lead: Any variable that changes the trapped air mass, the mixture strength or the timing moves brake power, brake thermal efficiency and emissions together. Weather matters too, so ratings are quoted at agreed reference air conditions, and a result measured on a hot day is corrected to those conditions before it is compared with the maker's figure. Tuning a vehicle for altitude, humidity or fuel quality uses the same ideas. The aim of this chapter is the shape of each curve and the reason for it, not just a list.
prereq: You need: the measured quantities from the chapters on performance parameters and fuel and air measurement, plus spark advance and knock from the ignition and combustion topics.

sections.h3: Speed, load and the shape of BSFC

blocks.text: Speed changes three things at once: the trapped air mass per cycle, friction and pumping loss. Indicated power rises with speed until breathing becomes the limit, then falls. Friction power rises faster than indicated power at high speed, so the gap between indicated and brake power grows.

Brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC) is fuel mass flow divided by brake power. Against speed it has a minimum at mid-speed: at low speed heat loss and friction are a large share of each cycle, and at high speed friction and pumping are large. Brake thermal efficiency is inversely proportional to BSFC, η<sub>bth</sub> = 3600 / (BSFC × LCV) with BSFC in kg/kWh and LCV in kJ/kg, so the speed of minimum BSFC is also the speed of maximum brake thermal efficiency.

Load has a similar curve. At low load, friction and auxiliary losses dominate, so BSFC is high. It falls as load rises and is lowest around three-quarter load. At full load, SI engines enrich the mixture and CI engines reach the smoke limit, so BSFC rises again.

blocks.where: ṁ<sub>f</sub> is fuel mass flow in kg/h and BP is brake power in kW, so BSFC is in kg/kWh. LCV is the lower calorific value of the fuel in kJ/kg.

sections.h3: Mixture strength, equivalence ratio and timing

blocks.text: Mixture strength is best described by the equivalence ratio φ, the actual fuel-air ratio over the stoichiometric fuel-air ratio: φ = (F/A)/(F/A)<sub>stoich</sub> = (A/F)<sub>stoich</sub>/(A/F). φ = 1 is stoichiometric, φ > 1 is rich and φ < 1 is lean.

For SI engines, maximum brake power comes from a slightly rich mixture, φ about 1.1: all the oxygen of the trapped air is used and the flame is fast. Best brake thermal efficiency comes from a slightly lean mixture, φ about 0.85 to 0.95: all the fuel burns, the burnt gas has a higher ratio of specific heats and less dissociation, less heat is lost to the walls, and at part load the throttle opens wider, cutting pumping loss. Very rich mixtures raise CO and HC; very lean mixtures burn slowly and can misfire. In CI engines the overall mixture is always lean, and power is limited by smoke.

Spark timing or injection timing sets where combustion occurs relative to top dead centre. Maximum brake torque (MBT) timing gives the highest brake torque at a given speed and mixture; it places the peak pressure roughly 15° after TDC. Too much advance raises peak pressure, causes knock and raises NOx. Too much retard burns the charge late in the expansion stroke, so less work is obtained, the exhaust temperature rises and HC can rise. Timing and mixture together set CO, HC and NOx (see Formation of CO, unburnt hydrocarbons and NOx).

Intake air density sets the trapped air mass. Density is ρ = p/(R T), where p is absolute pressure in Pa, T is absolute temperature in K and R is the gas constant for air, 287 J/(kg·K). A hot day or a high-altitude site lowers density, so brake power falls unless the engine is boosted. Humidity adds water vapour, which displaces some air and gives a small loss. Test standards correct the measured power to reference air temperature, pressure and humidity, so observed power and corrected power are different numbers; always state which one you mean (see the chapter on testing standards and pressure measurement).

Coolant and oil temperature matter. Cold coolant and cold oil raise friction and leave the fuel poorly vaporised, so BSFC rises. Very hot coolant can cause knock and thin the oil. Carbon deposits raise the compression ratio, create hot spots and restrict breathing, so they can cause knock and raise NOx. Valve clearance that is too tight holds the valve open, leaks compression and can burn the valve; too loose reduces lift and makes noise. Exhaust back pressure raises pumping work and reduces scavenging.

Fuel quality matters. Octane number controls SI knock; cetane number controls CI ignition delay; calorific value sets energy per kg; density sets the injected mass for a given volume. Compression ratio raises ideal efficiency but is limited by knock in SI engines and by peak pressure and NOx in diesels.

spec.aria: Two falling lines of brake power against intake temperature for 1.00 and 0.90 bar, with the reference point at 40 kW and the hot-day point at 34.27 kW.

examples.question: A naturally aspirated diesel engine gives 40 kW brake power at 25 °C and 1.00 bar on a standard day. It is retested on a hot afternoon at 40 °C and 0.90 bar. Assume brake power follows intake air density. Find the density ratio, the observed brake power and the percentage drop.
steps: Convert the temperatures to kelvin: T<sub>ref</sub> = 25 + 273 = 298 K and T<sub>test</sub> = 40 + 273 = 313 K.
Use the density ratio: (p<sub>test</sub> / p<sub>ref</sub>) × (T<sub>ref</sub> / T<sub>test</sub>) = (0.90 / 1.00) × (298 / 313) = 0.8569.
Multiply by the reference brake power: P<sub>obs</sub> = 40 × 0.8569 = 34.27 kW.
examples.answer: Density ratio = 0.857, observed brake power = 34.27 kW, a drop of 14.31 %.
examples.check:
p<sub>ref</sub> = 1.00
p<sub>test</sub> = 0.90
T<sub>ref</sub> = 298.0
T<sub>test</sub> = 313.0
P<sub>ref</sub> = 40.0
ratio = (p<sub>test</sub> / p<sub>ref</sub>) * (T<sub>ref</sub> / T<sub>test</sub>)
P<sub>obs</sub> = P<sub>ref</sub> * ratio
drop = (P<sub>ref</sub> - P<sub>obs</sub>) / P<sub>ref</sub> * 100.0
print(f'{ratio:.3f}')
print(f'{P<sub>obs</sub>:.2f}')
print(f'{drop:.2f}')

traps: Quoting an observed power as the engine's rating. Test standards correct to reference temperature, pressure and humidity, so always say whether a figure is observed or corrected.
Reversing the equivalence ratio. φ > 1 is rich, not lean; φ < 1 is lean, not rich.
Thinking best efficiency and best power occur at the same air-fuel ratio. Best power is slightly rich; best efficiency is lean.
Retarding timing only to reduce NOx. Too much retard lowers efficiency, raises exhaust temperature and can raise HC and CO.
Blaming the engine when a hot day or high altitude lowers observed power. Intake air density has fallen; the engine may be unchanged.

quiz.a: φ = (F/A)/(F/A)<sub>stoich</sub> = (A/F)<sub>stoich</sub>/(A/F). φ = 1 is stoichiometric, φ > 1 is rich and φ < 1 is lean.

quiz.q: Why does BSFC have a minimum at part load rather than at full load?
quiz.a: At low load, friction and heat losses are a large share of each cycle, so BSFC is high. Around three-quarter load these losses are spread over more work, so BSFC is lowest. At full load, enrichment or the smoke limit raises fuel use again.

quiz.q: An engine gives 60 kW at 1.00 bar and 300 K. It is tested at 0.92 bar and 315 K. Assume power follows air density. Find the density ratio and observed power.
Retarding the spark 10° from MBT timing at a fixed speed lowers brake thermal efficiency. Explain why, and say what happens to exhaust temperature and NOx.
quiz.a: At MBT the burn is centred so that peak pressure comes about 15° after TDC and the gas then expands fully. Retarded, more of the burn happens late in the expansion stroke, so less of the heat becomes work: torque and efficiency fall. The late heat leaves with the exhaust, so exhaust temperature rises; peak gas temperature falls, so NOx falls.

quiz.q: Why is maximum power obtained slightly rich while maximum efficiency is obtained lean?
quiz.a: A slightly rich mixture (φ about 1.1) makes sure all the oxygen of the trapped air is used and burns fast, so the most heat is released per cycle and power is highest. A lean mixture burns all its fuel, its gas has a higher ratio of specific heats and less dissociation, and less heat is lost, so a larger share of the heat becomes work; too lean slows combustion and can misfire.

quiz.q: Coolant temperature is kept too low. What happens to BSFC and why?
quiz.a: BSFC rises. Cold coolant and cold oil increase friction, and poor fuel vaporisation makes combustion less complete, so more fuel is needed for the same brake power.

quiz.q: On a hot, low-pressure day the observed power of a naturally aspirated engine is lower than its rated corrected power. Explain.
quiz.a: Hot air at low pressure has lower density, so each intake stroke traps less air mass. With less air, less fuel can be burned and brake power falls. The standard correction brings the observed result back to reference air conditions, so corrected power is higher than observed power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engine management systems continuously adjust fuel and spark or injection timing for air temperature, pressure and humidity, so the driver sees less of these effects than a fixed-calibration engine would show. Emission certification uses correction and driving cycles together, and real-driving tests add weather and traffic. Altitude kits for commercial vehicles and derating tables for generators are practical uses of density correction. Search next for SAE correction factors, engine derating, and altitude compensation in engine control units.
